order.subject: science
order.topic: Chemical reactions and conservation of mass
order.requests: Follow my lesson notes. I never want a key or explanation that says mass disappears or that gas has no mass. Use the counting table I use for atoms.

itemRequests.notes: Fill-in blanks like my old notes, with a word bank and a Stop and think box per section.
itemRequests.slides: One slide per big idea, plus a closed vs. open flask slide. Speaker notes should tell me what to ask the class.
itemRequests.quiz: 10 questions, my Know it / Use it / Explain it parts. At least one balancing question and one open vs. closed mass problem. Include a picture with no answer labels.

notes: Name, Date and Period lines across the top, then the title and a "Science 8 · Mr. Okafor" line
Bold directions in one or two short sentences right under the title
Questions numbered 1), 2), 3) straight through the whole document, across parts
Multiple-choice letters in parentheses: (A) (B) (C) (D); circle the letter
Quizzes split into three parts: Part 1 · Know it, Part 2 · Use it, Part 3 · Explain it; Explain it asks for complete sentences and names the words to use in bold
Guided notes: ⭐ Key idea headings, short fill-in sentences with one blank each, a 🤔 Stop and think question, and a word bank used "only if you get stuck"
Plain, short grade 8 sentences; everyday contexts (a rubber duck, popcorn, a named student who makes a claim to check)
Teacher key: the letter, a short reason in parentheses for math steps, and "Look for:" points for written answers

documents.title: Guided Notes: Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Mass
documents.directions: Fill in each blank as we go. Use the word bank only if you get stuck.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 1: Atoms are rearranged
sections.directions: Word bank: rearranged · created · destroyed · after · somewhere

questions.prompt: In a chemical reaction, atoms are ______________ into new substances.
questions.why: Atoms trade partners to make new substances.

questions.prompt: No atoms are ______________ and none are ______________.
questions.why: Either order of the two words is fine: "created ... destroyed" or "destroyed ... created".

questions.prompt: So the total mass before a reaction equals the total mass ______________ it.
questions.why: Same atoms before and after, so the same mass.

questions.prompt: When it looks like mass changed, the atoms went ______________: something got in or got out (usually a gas).
questions.why: Mr. Okafor's rule: we say "the atoms went somewhere."

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: A friend says, "When the candle burned, some of the mass just disappeared." How would you fix that sentence? Use the word atoms.
questions.answer: The atoms did not disappear; they went somewhere. They joined into new substances, like gases that went into the air, so the mass is still there, just not on the table.
questions.why: Look for: atoms named, the idea that they went somewhere (into the air as gas), never "the mass disappeared."

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 2: Reactants and products
sections.directions: Word bank: reactants · products · left · right · yields

questions.prompt: ______________ are the substances you start with.
questions.why: Reactants go in.

questions.prompt: They are written on the ______________ side of a chemical equation.
questions.why: "Left is what we start with."

questions.prompt: ______________ are the new substances that form. They are written on the ______________ side.
questions.why: Products come out, on the right of the arrow.

questions.prompt: The arrow (→) means "react to form" or "______________."
questions.why: A plus sign separates two reactants or two products.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, name the reactants and the product. How do you know which is which?
questions.answer: Reactants: H₂ (hydrogen) and O₂ (oxygen). Product: H₂O (water). The reactants are on the left of the arrow and the product is on the right.
questions.why: Look for: H₂ and O₂ as reactants, H₂O as the product, and "left / right of the arrow" as the reason.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 3: Signs of a chemical change
sections.directions: Word bank: new · precipitate · color · temperature · proof · physical

questions.prompt: A chemical change makes a ______________ substance.
questions.why: That is the test for every example: is there a new substance?

questions.prompt: A solid that forms when two clear liquids are mixed is called a ______________.
questions.why: Clue 2 on the list.

questions.prompt: Other clues: a gas forms, an unexpected ______________ change, a ______________ change without outside heating or cooling, or light or a new odor.
questions.why: The five clues: gas, precipitate, color, temperature, light or odor.

questions.prompt: One clue alone is not ______________.
questions.why: Bubbles from boiling water are a clue, but no new substance forms.

questions.prompt: Boiling water, melting ice and crushing a can are ______________ changes, because no new substance forms.
questions.why: Changes of state and changes of shape are physical.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: Water boiling on the stove makes bubbles. Is it a chemical change? Explain.
questions.answer: No. It is a physical change (a change of state). The bubbles are still water, just as a gas; no new substance forms.
questions.why: Look for: "physical", "no new substance", and that bubbles alone are not proof.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 4: Reading a formula and counting atoms
sections.directions: Word bank: subscript · coefficient · one · everything · table

questions.prompt: The ______________ is the small number after a symbol. It tells how many atoms of that element are in one molecule.
questions.why: H₂O: the small 2 means 2 hydrogen atoms.

questions.prompt: No subscript means ______________ atom.
questions.why: The O in H₂O has no subscript, so there is 1 oxygen atom.

questions.prompt: The ______________ is the big number in front. It tells how many molecules.
questions.why: 3H₂O means 3 molecules of water.

questions.prompt: In Ca(OH)₂, the 2 after the parentheses applies to ______________ inside them.
questions.why: Ca(OH)₂: 1 Ca, 2 O, 2 H.

questions.prompt: We always count atoms with a ______________: element, reactant side, product side.
questions.why: Mr. Okafor's counting table.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: Fill in the counting table for 3H₂O (just this one formula, in the "Reactant side" column). Show the multiplying.
questions.answer: H: 3 × 2 = 6 hydrogen atoms. O: 3 × 1 = 3 oxygen atoms.
questions.why: Look for: coefficient times subscript for each element; 6 H and 3 O.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 5: Balancing simple equations
sections.directions: Word bank: same · coefficients · subscript · recount · conservation

questions.prompt: A balanced equation has the ______________ number of atoms of each element on both sides.
questions.why: Atoms, not molecules: every row of the table matches.

questions.prompt: A balanced equation is ______________ of mass written in symbols.
questions.why: Same atoms on both sides means the same mass.

questions.prompt: Balance by changing ______________ only.
questions.why: Coefficients change how many molecules, not what the substance is.

questions.prompt: Never change a ______________: that changes the substance (H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, not water).
questions.why: The most common balancing mistake.

questions.prompt: Steps: count atoms in a table → pick an element that doesn't match → change a coefficient → ______________ everything → repeat until every row matches.
questions.why: Changing one coefficient can change more than one row, so recount all of them.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: Balance N₂ + H₂ → NH₃ by writing coefficients. Use the counting table to check it.
questions.answer: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. N: 2 on the reactant side, 2 on the product side. H: 6 on the reactant side, 6 on the product side.
questions.why: Look for: coefficients only (no subscripts changed), 1, 3, 2, and a table where both rows match.

sections.heading: ⭐ Key idea 6: Closed and open systems
sections.directions: Word bank: closed · open · escape · more · same

questions.prompt: A ______________ system lets nothing in or out, like a sealed flask or a zip bag.
questions.why: Nothing in, nothing out: the balance reading stays the same.

questions.prompt: In a closed system, the mass on the balance stays the ______________ before and after the reaction.
questions.why: Zip bag lab: 150.0 g before, 150.0 g after.

questions.prompt: An ______________ system lets matter in or out, like an open cup.
questions.why: Gas can leave, or a gas from the air can join in.

questions.prompt: In an open cup, a gas product can ______________, so the balance shows less mass after.
questions.why: Open cup lab: the CO₂ gas left the cup.

questions.prompt: When steel wool burns on a balance, iron atoms join with oxygen atoms from the air. The balance shows ______________ mass after the burning than before.
questions.why: Mass of steel wool + mass of oxygen used = mass of the iron oxide made.

questions.prompt: 🤔 Stop and think: Baking soda and vinegar in an open cup: 150.0 g before, 148.9 g after. What mass of gas escaped, and where did it go?
questions.answer: 150.0 g − 148.9 g = 1.1 g of carbon dioxide gas. It left the cup and went into the air. The atoms went somewhere; the mass did not disappear.
questions.why: Look for: 1.1 g, CO₂ (a gas) leaving the open cup, and gas having mass.
